title: Jason Alexander Apologizes to Courtney Stodden Over Inappropriate 2012 Sketch
excerpt: The Seinfeld actor expressed regret after Stodden called him out on Instagram for a Funny or Die sketch filmed when she was 17 years old.
body:
• Jason Alexander apologized for a 2012 sketch that made inappropriate jokes about Courtney Stodden when she was a minor.
  • Stodden accepted the apology but urged Alexander to support anti-child marriage initiatives.
  • The incident has brought attention to California Assembly Bill 1267, which aims to end child marriage.
  • Stodden advocates for legislative changes to protect minors from early marriage.
Key Takeaways
  • Jason Alexander apologized for a 2012 sketch involving Courtney Stodden when she was a minor.
  • The sketch featured inappropriate jokes about Stodden's body and future sexual intentions.
  • Stodden accepted the apology but urged Alexander to support anti-child marriage efforts.
  • The incident highlights California Assembly Bill 1267, aiming to end child marriage.
  • Stodden advocates for legislative change to protect minors from early marriage.

Jason Alexander, the 66-year-old actor best known for playing George Costanza on Seinfeld, has issued a public apology to Courtney Stodden after a 2012 Funny or Die sketch resurfaced in which he made sexual comments about her body while she was still a minor.

"Looking back at the comedy sketch in which Ms. Stodden and I participated in 2012, I completely agree that it was inappropriate and I truly regret it," Alexander said in a statement shared with Entertainment Weekly on Tuesday. "But more importantly, I am deeply sorry for any harm or distress it has caused Ms. Stodden. I offer her my sincerest apologies."

What Was in the Sketch

The sketch, titled "The Donny Clay Show With Courtney Stodden," was a Funny or Die skit that parodied daytime talk shows. Stodden was 17 at the time of filming. In the sketch, Alexander — who is also credited as a co-writer on IMDb — repeatedly rubbed his cellphone across a bikini-clad Stodden's chest while saying there was "no signal" in her head but "plenty of signal" in her chest. He also joked that when she turned 18, he would like to take her behind the couch and "have his way" with her.

The controversy reignited on July 20 when Stodden, now 31, shared a still from the sketch on Instagram with a lengthy caption.

"I was 17 years old in this photo. The older I get, the more impossible this is to understand. I was the only child in the room. I felt so alone."

— Courtney Stodden, via Instagram

Stodden wrote that as a minor she "didn't have the legal power to decide whether I wanted to participate," adding that the contracts were signed by adults and the paycheck went to her then-husband, Doug Hutchison.

Stodden Accepts Apology, Calls for Action

In a follow-up conversation with TMZ, Stodden said she accepts Alexander's apology and hopes it came from a genuine place of reflection. But she pushed for the moment to carry real-world weight.

"I believe the most meaningful apology is one that creates change. I would encourage him to support and donate to Unchained At Last, an organization I'm proud to advocate alongside that is leading the fight to end child marriage in the United States."

— Courtney Stodden, to TMZ

Stodden first gained public attention in 2011 when, at age 16, she married actor Doug Hutchison, then 51. The marriage was legal because her parents gave permission. The couple separated and reconciled multiple times before splitting for good in 2016, with their divorce finalized in 2020. Stodden has since remarried husband Jared Safier and become an advocate against child marriage.

Child Marriage Advocacy Gains Momentum
›Courtney Stodden married at 16 with parental consent.
›California Assembly Bill 1267 seeks to raise marriage age to 18.
›34 U.S. states allow underage marriage with parental permission.
›4 states have no minimum age for marriage with waivers.
Data from Equality Now and California Assembly Bill 1267

A Broader Reckoning With Hollywood's Past

The episode comes amid a wider cultural conversation about how the entertainment industry has treated minors. Stodden's Instagram caption also included a call to support California Assembly Bill 1267, which aims to permanently end child marriage by setting the minimum legal age for marriage in California to 18 with no exceptions, according to Fox News.

In a 2025 interview with People, Stodden noted that underage marriage remains legal with parental permission in 34 U.S. states, with four states requiring no minimum age at all with a parental or judicial waiver. The organization Equality Now has corroborated these figures.

"I don't want this to happen to anyone else, and it scares me," Stodden told People at the time.

What's Next

While Alexander's statement appeared to close the immediate dispute, Stodden has made clear she wants the conversation to extend beyond personal accountability. Her advocacy for Unchained At Last and the California bill signals that she intends to keep pushing for legislative change. The status of AB 1267 in the California legislature remains a key marker to watch in the months ahead.
